title: Your code, at an address you can give away
summary: Push last season's free-build code to a repo on the family GitHub account, write a README a human can actually follow, then circle one shop idea and sketch the first unit.
materials: laptop with Python and the editor from week 1
the code folder from last season's free build, which has never had git run in it
the family GitHub account, with a parent signed in
phone or camera for photos of the build in use
the Season 2 free build itself, for those photos
the shop idea page opened in week 1
graph paper, pencil and a ruler for the prototype sketch

steps.title: Ask, imagine, plan
steps.body:
The design loop, same six moves as always: ask, imagine, plan, build, test, fix.

Ask: what makes a piece of work real? Two weeks ago your Python moved off the micro:bit and onto the laptop. Last week the actual USACO grader read a program you planned, with a parent at the keyboard. Both of those still live in small places: your machine, and one grader's memory of one submission. Work that lives only on your laptop is a rehearsal. Shipped somewhere other people can reach it, it becomes real. That idea has a name from today: ship it.

Imagine: somebody you have never met types an address into a browser and lands on your project. Your code is there. Photos of the thing you built are there. So is a page of instructions you wrote for them, not for the machine. They read it, they run it, and it works, and you are not in the room. Hold that picture, because next week a real person who was never in the room tries exactly that.

Plan: three jobs, in this order. One, the repo: last season's free build code gets a home on GitHub. Git has never been run in that folder, so it gets the same start your season folder got in week 1, an init and a first camp, and then the whole thing goes up. The commits you cut in your season folder stay exactly where they are; that folder gets its own turn later in the season. Two, the README: the page a human reads first, written for the next person, who is usually future you. Three, the shop: the idea page you opened in week 1 gets one idea circled and a first unit sketched.

One honest thing before any of it. GitHub's own rules say an account holder has to be 13 or older, so the account is a parent's account, signed in, with the parent sitting beside you. The plan is yours, the words are yours, the typing is yours. The account is theirs and their name is on the door, which is exactly why what you push has to be something you would both be happy for a stranger to read. Before you push, decide together whether this repo is public to the whole internet or shared only with people you invite. Both are real choices, and the difference is who the address opens for. Public means anyone you hand it to can read it. Private means only the people the account invites can, and everybody else who types it gets a page saying there is nothing there. Next week somebody who was never in the room follows your README on their own computer, so if you go private today, that person has to be invited before then. Decide it now, out loud, not on the day.

Five minutes on your typing site. Warm up on the home row, then drill today's words until your fingers stop hunting: git, status, add, commit, push, origin, main, README. Then the punctuation this week leans on, because a typo in any of these stops the command dead: the hyphen for a flag like -m, the double quote at both ends of a message, and the single dot that means this whole folder. Type the line git commit -m "why I changed it" ten times. You will type it for real in about ten minutes.

figure.alt: Typing an address asks a lookup service which machine it belongs to; your laptop then sends that server a short request and receives a copy of the page back, while the original stays on the server, which is why many people can read it at once.

steps.title: Where a website actually lives
steps.body:
An address on the internet feels like a place, the way a street address does. It is not. It is a set of directions to a computer.

When you type an address, your laptop first asks a lookup service which machine that name belongs to, and gets back a number, the machine's address on the network. Then your laptop sends that machine a short, polite request: please send me this page. The machine sends a copy back. Nothing travelled from there to here the way a parcel does. Your laptop got a copy and the machine still has the original, which is why a million people can read the same page at once without wearing it out.

That machine is a server, and a server is just a computer that never sleeps. No screen, no mouse, stacked on a shelf with thousands of others in a building with loud air conditioning, doing one thing: waiting for requests and answering them. Ten requests a second is a quiet day for one of them, and that is around a million answers before it gets dark.

So when a site is down, this is what has happened: some machine in some building stopped answering, or the lookup failed, or the wires between you and it are cut. Nothing vanished. Something stopped replying. And today your project joins the pile of things those machines are ready to hand out to anyone who asks.

figure.alt: A scale of 1 to 100,000 means one centimetre on the map equals 100,000 centimetres, one kilometre, on the ground. The straight-line distance between two points uses a right triangle: across and up are the short sides, and the real distance is the long side.

steps.title: A map's scale is a shrunk triangle
steps.body:
Your prototype sketch sits at a scale: one centimetre on paper stands for some real number of centimetres on the object. A map works the identical way, just at a far bigger ratio.

A map marked 1 to 100,000 means one centimetre on the page equals 100,000 centimetres, one kilometre, on the ground. Two towns four centimetres apart on that map sit four real kilometres apart.

Finding the straight-line distance between two points that are not lined up east-west or north-south uses the right triangle you already know. The across distance and the up distance are the two short sides. The real distance is the long side, found the way you would find it on paper, then multiplied out by the scale.

Draw your prototype at a stated scale this week. Measure two points on your sketch, work out the real distance with the triangle, then check it against a tape measure on the actual part.

figure.alt: git init and commits build a trail only on your laptop. git remote add origin points that folder at an empty repo on GitHub, git branch -M main names the branch main, and git push -u origin main sends every camp up to the address a browser can open.

items.s: git remote add origin: points laptop at new home
git branch -M main: names the branch main
git push -u origin main: sends camp up

steps.title: Give the repo a home
steps.body:
A parent signs in to the family GitHub account first. You drive the keyboard from there, and they stay next to you until the last command has run.

Name the repo before you make it, on paper. Short, lowercase, hyphens instead of spaces, and it says what the thing is: something in the shape of night-light-v1 or dice-roller. Three rules on the name and on the words inside the repo, and they are not suggestions: no last name, no school name, no street or house number. A neutral handle and a neutral repo name means the address can be handed to anyone at all.

On GitHub, with the parent's account signed in, make a new empty repository with that name. Do not let it add a README for you; you are writing that yourself in the next step. Choose public or private together, out loud, before you click.

Now open a terminal in last season's free build folder, the one holding the code you are publishing. Run `git status` first, always, so you know what git thinks is going on. This folder has never met git, so it answers `fatal: not a git repository (or any of the parent directories): .git`. That is not a fault, it is git telling you the truth: nothing here remembers anything yet. Give it a memory with `git init`, run `git status` again to see every file listed as untracked, then pack them with `git add .` and cut the first camp with a `git commit` whose message says why, not what: stopped the light flickering when the battery is low beats changed code.

Then run the three lines GitHub shows you on the empty repo page, in the order it prints them: the `git remote add origin` line that points your folder at its new home, then `git branch -M main`, which names your branch main so it matches the name GitHub is expecting, then `git push -u origin main`, which sends everything up. Do not skip the middle one. Depending on which options a grown-up ticked when git was installed, your branch may still be called master, and a push to a main that does not exist dies on `error: src refspec main does not match any` and explains nothing else. `git branch -M main` costs nothing when the branch is already called main.

When the push finishes, open the address in a browser and look. Your commit message is there with its date, and it is camp one on this project's trail. Every camp you cut here from now on lands on that same page, and anyone the address reaches can walk it.
checklist: The repo name has no last name, no school and no address in it, and a parent's account made it
We said public or private out loud and agreed before clicking, and if it is private we wrote down who has to be invited before next week
git status ran before anything else, and every commit message says why rather than what
The push finished and the browser shows my commits with their messages

steps.title: A README for a human
steps.body:
The machine already knows how to run your code. The README is not for the machine. It is for the next person, and the next person is usually future you, six months from now, having forgotten everything.

Make a file called README.md in the project folder and answer four questions, in this order, in your own words:

1. What is this? One or two sentences in plain language, no jargon. What it does, and what it was for.

2. What do you need? The parts and the software. Say the actual versions where you know them.

3. How do I run it? Numbered steps, starting from the very first thing a person does, which is opening a folder. Not just run it. Every step, in order, including the boring ones.

4. What should I see? What happens when it works, so a reader can tell success from a silent failure.

Then photos. Two or three of the build in use, lighting up or moving or doing its job. The privacy rules from last season still stand: no faces, no last names, no school, nothing in the background with an address on it. Hands are fine. Put the photos in the folder and link them in the README so they show on the page.

One more thing about the words. Your free build was made for someone, and the person it was for does not need naming on the open internet. Write a present for someone in my family and the README loses nothing.

Now the rehearsal, which is the whole point of this step. Push the README, open the page in the browser, and read it top to bottom as if you had never seen this project before. Hands in your lap. Every place where you had to remember something the page did not say, mark it, then fix it and push again. Next week a real person does this test, and only the page can help them.
checklist: The README answers all four questions, and the run steps start from opening a folder
Two or three photos of the build in use are on the page, with no faces, names or addresses
Nobody the project was made for is named on the page
I read my own README as a stranger would, hands off the keyboard, and fixed every place I had to remember something it did not say
The fixed README is committed and pushed, so the page a visitor sees is the fixed one

figure.alt: A v0.1 sketch is a real plan: the part drawn with measurements on its edges, a battery, if there is one, shown in a fixed holder, and a materials list down the side with every price starred if it was looked up.

items.s: every part labelled with the sketch's own words

steps.title: Circle one idea and sketch unit number one
steps.body:
Open the shop idea page from week 1 and read the whole list out loud, including the silly ones. Then put every idea through three questions, and write the answers next to each one:

1. Could you make ten of these, by yourself, in a few evenings? Not one. Ten. A shop needs stock.

2. Can every material fit inside the seed loan your family has set? If you do not know what a material costs, that is a thing to find out, not a thing to guess forever.

3. Would somebody who is not related to you hand over their own money for it? Be hard about this one. Family will buy anything you make. Strangers will not, and the whole point of this season is people who owe you nothing.

Now circle one. Not the best idea in the world: the best idea you can hold in your hand by week 5. Write one sentence under the circle saying what it is and who it is for.

Then sketch unit number one on graph paper. Not a mood picture, a plan. Real measurements on the edges. Every part labelled. A materials list down the side with a price against each line and a total at the bottom, and a star next to any price you actually looked up rather than guessed. If your idea has an electronic part, mark on the sketch where the battery lives and how it is held, because a battery holder is a design decision and a loose coin cell around a small child is not allowed.

Write today's date on the sketch and label it v0.1. Version numbers are honest: v0.1 means first try, expected to change. Next week you pitch this to the family, and they will cross-examine the plan, never the choice. The choice is yours.
checklist: Every idea on the page has answers written next to it for all three questions
Exactly one idea is circled, with one sentence saying what it is and who it is for
The sketch has real measurements, labelled parts and a materials list with a price against every line
Prices I looked up are starred and prices I guessed are not, so I can tell them apart later
The sketch is dated and labelled v0.1

steps.title: Bug diary
steps.body:
One line for each thing that did not work the first time and what you tried. Today's usual suspects, none of which mean anything is broken.

The push is rejected and the message mentions permission: the browser is signed in but the terminal is not, so the account that owns the repo and the account the terminal is using are two different things. A parent sorts that one out with you.

The push says src refspec main does not match any: your branch is not called main, it is called master, so there is no main to send. `git branch -M main` renames it and the push works. Run `git branch --show-current` if you want to see the name for yourself.

A commit says there is nothing to commit: you changed files but never ran `git add`, so git is looking at an empty tray.

The remote already exists: you ran the `git remote add origin` line twice. Harmless, and `git remote -v` shows what it points at now.

The photos do not appear on the page: the file name in the README does not match the real file name, and capital letters count on a server even when they do not on your laptop.

And the one that is not a bug at all: the README looks plain next to your editor. That is markdown doing its job, and it is what every project on the site looks like.

steps.title: Show it
steps.prompt: The repo address, typed out in full, plus a screenshot of the README page as a visitor sees it with the photos showing, plus a photo of your dated v0.1 sketch with its materials list.
